mappings.note: Fill-in pairing the two characters with their traits; LO-5 names identifying characters. Rejected LO-6, which is for open written responses.
Turns on the meaning of 'croak' and its shared use for frog and raven - word meaning from context, LO-11. Rejected LO-5: nothing about plot or character is being retrieved.
Who was perched on the limb: a stated detail. LO-5, not LO-6, as no inference is required.
What the fox complimented - stated detail. LO-5; the distractors test close reading, not reasoning, so not LO-6.
Why the Raven forgets his croak is never stated; the pupil must infer it from vanity. LO-6's written response over LO-5.
Names Reynard: stated detail. LO-5.
Tone of the compliment (sarcastic) is nowhere labelled in the poem - pure reading between the lines, so LO-6 not LO-5.
Five-mark recount of how the flattery worked, step by step: LO-5's sequence of events, written as the coherent piece LO-14 asks for. Rejected LO-6 because the steps are all on the page.
What was in the beak: stated detail. LO-5.
Marked False even though the fox says so in the poem, so the pupil must separate flattery from fact - reading between the lines, LO-6 rather than LO-5's detail check.
Reynard's reason for calling pride unwise is implied by his trick; LO-6 for the inference, LO-14 for the 5-mark coherent answer.
The compliment itself is quoted in the poem - detail retrieval, LO-5 not LO-6.
True/false characterisation of the Raven. LO-5 covers identifying characters.
Asks why the moral is a surprise coming from the cheat - irony, entirely between the lines. LO-6 with LO-14 for the extended answer; LO-5 rejected as the irony is not stated.
The fox's suggestion is stated. LO-5 detail retrieval.
True/false on the outcome of the plot - sequence of events, LO-5.

'Imagine someone praises you too much - how would you react' asks the pupil to narrate a hypothetical of their own, which is LO-12's imaginary situation in writing. Rejected LO-6: no text is being comprehended.
Second half ('how did he use this admiration') asks for the fox's unstated purpose; LO-6 for the inference, LO-14 for the 5-mark write-up.
True/false against the stated setting (a limb, not a wall). LO-5 detail verification.

Rhyme-pair hunt. Cited at competency level because the 16-outcome Class 6 frame has no poetic-device outcome at all - C-ENG1.1 is the competency that owns poems and their sound. Rejected its LO-2 ('Recite and share poems...') because nothing is recited here, and rejected LO-11, which is about meaning, not sound.
The Raven's reaction to the praise is narrated in the poem; LO-5 for the character detail, LO-14 for the 5-mark coherent answer. Rejected LO-6 as nothing needs inferring.
True/false on where the flattery begins - the sequence of ideas, LO-5.

Antonym table plus 'make sentences of your own': LO-11 is the antonyms outcome verbatim, LO-12 the meaningful sentences built from them. Rejected LO-5/LO-6 - this is a vocabulary drill, not comprehension of the poem.
Consequences of opening the beak are the poem's own chain of events; LO-5 for the sequence, LO-14 for the 5-mark piece. Rejected LO-6.
What Reynard noticed (the morsel) - stated detail, LO-5.
The lesson is stated in the closing lines, so LO-5's main idea rather than LO-6; LO-14 for the 5-mark answer.
The fox's motive for complimenting is withheld until the end - inference, LO-6 over LO-5.
Theme traced through the characters' actions - LO-5's main ideas and characters, written up coherently per LO-14.
How the Raven showed his pleasure - stated detail, LO-5.
Describes the whole exchange in order; LO-5's sequence of events with LO-14 for the sustained answer. Rejected LO-6 as the exchange is on the page.
What the fox did afterwards - sequence of events, LO-5.
'What role does flattery play' asks for a function the poem never names; LO-6 for the inference, LO-14 for the extended answer.
What the Raven should have remembered is a judgement the pupil supplies; LO-6 over LO-5.
Cause-and-effect analysis of pride to downfall; LO-6 for the reasoning, LO-14 for the 5-mark shape.
Why he began to sing requires joining the flattery to his forgetting - inference, so LO-6.
The significance of the closing laugh is unstated; LO-6 for reading between the lines, LO-14 for the 5-mark answer.
Pairs each animal's defining trait against the plot - LO-5's identifying of characters. Rejected LO-6: both traits are demonstrated in the text.
Theme and its consequences - the poem's main idea, LO-5, with LO-14 for the extended write-up.
Unpacks a quoted line into 'lesson' and 'price', neither labelled in the poem; LO-6 plus LO-14 for the 5-mark answer.
'Analyze how the Fox is portrayed' goes past naming traits to how the poem builds them - LO-6, not LO-5; LO-14 for the sustained piece.
Applies an outside Ruskin quotation to the poem - going beyond the text, LO-6, with LO-14 for the argued 5-mark answer. Rejected LO-7: the quotation is given, not researched.
Impact of pride on the Raven's fate is an interpretive claim; LO-6 with LO-14.

Two demands: evaluate the moral (LO-6's critical response) and judge its relevance today, which is LO-5's 'relate them to personal experience'. Rejected LO-14 to keep the citation to what the item actually asks.

Asks how the poem's structure - rhythm and rhyme - carries its message. Cited at competency level because the Class 6 frame's 16 outcomes contain no poetic-form outcome; LO-6 rejected as it covers questions on content, not on verse form.
Invents an alternate ending: LO-12 names narrating imaginary situations, LO-13 the drafting of a paragraph from print clues. Rejected LO-6 - nothing in the given poem is being comprehended.
Lists the fox's traits, all evidenced in the poem - LO-5's identifying of characters rather than LO-6's inference.
Reads an action back into personality - an inference the poem does not make. LO-6 over LO-5.
The stem says 'can be inferred', which is LO-6 by definition; LO-5 rejected.

Imagery question. Competency-level citation because no outcome in this 16-outcome frame reaches literary device; LO-6 rejected as it is about answering content questions, and LO-11 as imagery is not word meaning.
Generalises from the poem to how pride works in social life - going beyond the text, LO-6 rather than LO-5's stated main idea.
